p.src: Meanwhile, Han Dang and Zhou Tai learned that the First Emperor had moved his camps to cooler ground and hurried to report this to Lu Xun. Lu Xun was delighted and personally led troops out to observe the enemy's movements. On level ground he saw a camp of scarcely more than ten thousand men, most of them old or infirm, beneath a great banner proclaiming, “Vanguard Wu Ban.” Zhou Tai said, “In my eyes, defeating soldiers like these would be child's play. Let General Han and me divide into two columns and attack them. If we fail, I will gladly submit to military punishment.” Lu Xun watched for a long while, then pointed with his whip and said, “A faint aura of slaughter rises from the valley ahead. An ambush must be concealed there; these weak troops have been placed on the plain merely to lure us out. On no account are any of you to go out.” When the generals heard this, they all took him for a coward.

p.src: The next day, Wu Ban led his troops before the pass and challenged the defenders, flaunting their might and hurling ceaseless abuse. Many stripped off their clothes and armor, baring their bodies; some slept, while others sat about. Xu Sheng and Ding Feng entered Lu Xun's tent and reported, “The Shu troops insult us beyond endurance! We beg leave to go out and strike them!” Lu Xun laughed. “You gentlemen rely only on hot-blooded valor and know nothing of the military methods of Sun and Wu. This is their scheme to lure us out. Within three days their deception will become plain.” Xu Sheng said, “In three days their camps will already be firmly established. How could we attack them then?” Lu Xun replied, “I want them to move their camps.” The generals withdrew with derisive smiles. Three days later, Lu Xun assembled the generals atop the pass to survey the scene, and they saw that Wu Ban's troops had withdrawn. Lu Xun pointed and said, “Now the aura of slaughter is rising. Liu Bei will surely emerge from the valley.” Before he had finished speaking, the Shu troops appeared, fully armed and properly accoutered, escorting the First Emperor past. At the sight, the soldiers of Wu were terrified out of their wits. Lu Xun said, “This is precisely why I would not heed you gentlemen and attack Wu Ban. Now that the troops in ambush have emerged, I shall certainly defeat Shu within ten days.” The generals all said, “If Shu was to be defeated, it should have been done at the outset. Now their linked camps extend five or six hundred li, and we have faced each other for seven or eight months. They have secured every strategic point—how can they possibly be defeated?” Lu Xun said, “You gentlemen do not understand the art of war. Bei is a formidable hero of the age, rich in cunning and strategy. When his army first assembled, its discipline and organization were exacting. But they have now been encamped for a long time without finding any opening against us; their soldiers are weary and their spirits frustrated. Today is precisely the time to take them.” Only then did the generals sigh in admiration and submit to his judgment. A later poet wrote in praise:

p.src: Meanwhile, having settled his plan to defeat Shu, Lu Xun wrote a memorial and sent an envoy to Sun Quan, declaring that Shu could be broken within days. After reading it, Sun Quan rejoiced. “That Jiangdong should possess another extraordinary man like this—what have I to fear? The generals all submitted memorials calling him cowardly, but I alone refused to believe them. Now, judging by his words, he is indeed no coward.” He thereupon raised a great force of Wu troops and sent them as reinforcements.

p.src: Meanwhile, at Xiaoting the First Emperor dispatched his entire naval force downstream, establishing water camps along the river as he advanced deep into Wu territory. Huang Quan remonstrated, “For a naval force descending the river, advance is easy but retreat is difficult. I beg to serve as the vanguard. Your Majesty should remain with the rear division, so that no mishap can possibly occur.” The First Emperor said, “The Wu rebels have lost their nerve. As I drive straight onward, what obstacle can there be?” The officers earnestly remonstrated, but the First Emperor would not listen. He divided his forces into two columns, ordering Huang Quan to command the troops north of the river and guard against an attack from Wei. The First Emperor personally commanded the armies south of the river, establishing camps on both banks as a base for further advances. Spies discovered this and reported through the night to the ruler of Wei: the Shu army was attacking Wu, erecting palisades and linking its camps over more than seven hundred li, with over forty encampments, all pitched beside mountains and forests. Huang Quan now commands troops on the north bank, sending scouts more than a hundred li out each day; his purpose is unknown.

p.src: When the ruler of Wei heard this, he threw back his head and laughed. “Liu Bei is going to be defeated.” The assembled ministers asked why. The ruler of Wei said, “Liu Xuande understands nothing of warfare. How can camps linked over seven hundred li possibly withstand an enemy? To spread troops over plains and wetlands, among hazards and difficult ground, is one of warfare's greatest taboos. Xuande will surely be defeated at the hands of Lu Xun of Eastern Wu. Within ten days the news will certainly arrive.” The ministers still did not believe him and all urged that troops be assigned in readiness. The ruler of Wei said, “If Lu Xun wins, he will surely mobilize all of Eastern Wu's forces to seize Xichuan. When the Wu armies have gone far away and their realm lies empty, I shall make a show of sending troops to assist them in battle, while our three columns advance together. Eastern Wu will then be ours for the taking.” All bowed in admiration. The ruler of Wei ordered Cao Ren to lead one army out through Ruxu, Cao Xiu another through Dongkou, and Cao Zhen a third through Nanjun, saying, “The three armies shall agree upon a date to join forces and make a surprise attack on Eastern Wu. I shall come afterward in person to support you.” The deployments were thus settled.

p.src: We shall say no more for now of the Wei attack on Wu. Meanwhile, Ma Liang reached Shu and went in to see Kongming. Presenting the map, he said, “The camps have now been moved and extend on both sides of the river for seven hundred li. More than forty camps have been established, all beside streams and ravines where the woods grow thick. His Majesty ordered me to bring this map for the Chancellor to examine.” When Kongming had finished examining it, he struck the table and cried in dismay, “Who advised His Majesty to pitch his camps in this fashion? That man deserves to be beheaded!” Ma Liang said, “It was all His Majesty's own doing, not another man's counsel.” Kongming sighed. “The destiny of the Han is ended!” Ma Liang asked why. Kongming said, “To establish camps spread over plains and wetlands, amid hazards and difficult ground, is a great taboo among commanders. If the enemy attacks with fire, how can the situation be saved? And how could camps linked over seven hundred li possibly withstand an enemy? Disaster is close at hand! This is precisely why Lu Xun has held his ground and refused battle. You must hasten back to see the Emperor and have all the camps relocated. They must not remain as they are.” Ma Liang said, “What are we to do if the Wu army has already won?” Kongming said, “Lu Xun will not dare pursue. Chengdu can be kept safe.” Ma Liang asked, “Why will Lu Xun not pursue?” Kongming said, “Because he fears the Wei army will strike him from the rear. If His Majesty suffers a reverse, he should seek refuge in Baidi City. When I entered Shu, I already concealed a hundred thousand troops at Yufupu.” Ma Liang was astonished. “I have passed through Yufupu several times and never seen a single soldier. Why does the Chancellor tell such an untruth?” Kongming said, “You will see them in due course. There is no need for further questions.” Ma Liang obtained a memorial and hurried with all speed toward the imperial camp. Kongming himself returned to Chengdu and deployed troops to provide support.

p.src: Meanwhile, when Lu Xun saw that the Shu troops had grown lax and no longer kept watch, he took his seat in the command tent and assembled officers and soldiers of every rank to receive orders. “Since receiving my commission, I have never once given battle. Now, having observed the Shu army, I know its situation well enough and intend first to seize one camp on the south bank of the river. Who dares take it?” Before he had finished speaking, Han Dang, Zhou Tai, Ling Tong, and others stepped forward at once. “We are willing to go.” Lu Xun dismissed them all without employing them and summoned only Chunyu Dan, a junior officer standing below. “I give you five thousand troops. Go and seize the fourth camp south of the river, which is held by the Shu general Fu Tong. You must succeed tonight. I shall personally lead troops to support you.” After Chunyu Dan had led his troops away, Lu Xun summoned Xu Sheng and Ding Feng. “Each of you is to lead three thousand troops and station yourselves five li outside the camp. If Chunyu Dan returns defeated with enemy troops pursuing him, go out and rescue him, but do not pursue the enemy in turn.” The two generals went away to deploy their troops.

p.src: Now Chunyu Dan led his troops forward at dusk. By the time he reached the Shu encampment, it was already past the third watch. Dan ordered his soldiers to charge in with a great clamor. From within the Shu camp, Fu Tong led his men out to meet them and leveled his spear straight at Chunyu Dan. Unable to withstand him, Dan wheeled his horse and fled. Suddenly, tremendous battle cries arose, and a body of troops blocked his path. At their head was the general Zhao Rong. Dan fought his way through and escaped, but lost more than half his men. As he fled, another body of tribal troops emerged from behind the mountain and barred his way, led by the foreign chieftain Shamoke. Dan fought desperately and broke free, while three forces pursued him from behind. When he had gone five li from the camp, the Wu generals Xu Sheng and Ding Feng attacked from opposite sides. The Shu troops withdrew, allowing them to rescue Chunyu Dan and escort him back to camp. Dan, still carrying an arrow wound, went before Lu Xun and asked forgiveness. Lu Xun said, “The fault is not yours. I merely wished to test the enemy’s true strength. I have now settled upon a plan to defeat Shu.” Xu Sheng and Ding Feng said, “The Shu army is too powerful to defeat. We shall only lose soldiers and generals to no purpose.” Lu Xun laughed. “Only Zhuge Liang could see through this plan of mine. By Heaven’s favor he is not here, and so I shall accomplish a great victory.” He then assembled officers and men of every rank to receive their orders. Zhu Ran was to advance by water; when a strong southeast wind rose on the following afternoon, he was to load boats with thatching grass and carry out the plan. Han Dang was to lead one force against the north bank of the river, and Zhou Tai another against the south bank. Each man was to carry a bundle of thatching grass concealing sulfur and saltpeter, as well as tinder and a spear or sword, and all were to advance together. Upon reaching the Shu camps, they were to set fire to them with the wind. Of Shu’s forty camps, they were to burn only twenty, setting fire to every other camp. Every force was to carry dry provisions and was forbidden to retreat even briefly. They were to pursue and attack by day and night, stopping only when Liu Bei had been captured. The generals received their orders, each learned his part in the plan, and departed.

p.src: Meanwhile, the First Emperor was in his imperial camp pondering how to defeat Wu when he suddenly saw the central army’s banners before his tent fall of themselves, though there was no wind. He asked Cheng Ji, “What omen is this?” Cheng Ji replied, “Could the Wu troops be coming to raid our camp tonight?” The First Emperor said, “They were utterly defeated last night. How would they dare come again?” Cheng Ji said, “But what if Lu Xun was merely testing us?” While they were speaking, a report came that Wu troops had been seen from the mountain, all moving eastward along the slopes. The First Emperor said, “Those are decoy troops.” He ordered the army to remain still, then sent Guan Xing and Zhang Bao out on patrol with five hundred horsemen each. At dusk, Guan Xing returned and reported, “Fire has broken out in the camp north of the river.” The First Emperor urgently ordered Guan Xing to the north bank and Zhang Bao to the south to discover the truth: “If the Wu troops arrive, report back at once.”

p.src: The two generals accepted the command and departed. At the first watch, a southeast wind suddenly sprang up. Presently, flames rose from the camp to the left of the imperial encampment. Just as they were about to go to its aid, the camp to the right of the imperial encampment also caught fire. The wind was fierce and the flames spread swiftly; even the trees caught fire. Tremendous battle cries arose. The soldiers and horses from both camps poured out and rushed into the imperial encampment. The troops in the imperial encampment trampled one another, and the dead were beyond counting. Wu troops then attacked from the rear in numbers no one could reckon. The First Emperor hastily mounted and fled toward Feng Xi’s camp, only to see flames towering into the sky from within it. Both north and south of the river were lit as brightly as day. Feng Xi mounted in alarm and fled with several dozen horsemen, but ran straight into the army of the Wu general Xu Sheng and engaged it in battle. Seeing this, the First Emperor wheeled his horse and fled westward. Xu Sheng abandoned Feng Xi and led his troops in pursuit. As the First Emperor fled in panic, an army blocked his way ahead. It was led by the Wu general Ding Feng. The two forces attacked him from both sides. The First Emperor was greatly alarmed. There was no way out in any direction. Suddenly, tremendous battle cries arose, and a body of troops broke into the encirclement. It was Zhang Bao, who rescued the First Emperor and led the imperial guards away at speed. As they went, another force arrived ahead. It was the Shu general Fu Tong, who joined his troops to theirs and continued onward. The Wu troops caught up from behind. The First Emperor reached a mountain called Mount Ma’an. Zhang Bao and Fu Tong urged him to climb it, but once he had reached the summit, battle cries rose again below: Lu Xun’s main army had surrounded Mount Ma’an. Zhang Bao and Fu Tong defended the mountain pass to the death. From afar, the First Emperor saw unending firelight across the countryside, while corpses lay heaped upon one another and floated downriver in such numbers that they choked the stream.

p.src: The next day, the Wu troops set fire to the mountain from every side. The soldiers fled wildly, and the First Emperor was stricken with panic. Suddenly, a general with several horsemen charged up the mountain through the flames. When they looked, it was Guan Xing. Guan Xing prostrated himself and pleaded, “The flames are closing in from every side; we cannot remain here long. Your Majesty must hasten to Baidi City, where you may gather your forces once more.” The First Emperor said, “Who dares cover our retreat?” Fu Tong replied, “I am willing to hold them off at the cost of my life!” At dusk that day, with Guan Xing in front, Zhang Bao in the center, and Fu Tong left to guard the rear, they protected the First Emperor and fought their way down the mountain. When the Wu troops saw the First Emperor fleeing, all were eager to claim the honor. Each led a mighty force westward in pursuit, their numbers seeming to blot out heaven and cover the earth. The First Emperor ordered his soldiers to strip off their robes and armor, heap them across the road, and burn them to cut off the pursuing army. While they were still fleeing, tremendous battle cries arose, and the Wu general Zhu Ran led a force from the riverbank and blocked their path. The First Emperor cried, “Here is where I shall die!” Guan Xing and Zhang Bao spurred their horses and charged, but a storm of arrows drove them back. Both were badly wounded and could not break through. Battle cries rose again behind them: Lu Xun was leading his great army out of the mountain valley to attack.

p.src: As the First Emperor was overcome with panic, the sky had begun to brighten faintly. Suddenly, tremendous battle cries arose ahead; Zhu Ran’s soldiers tumbled one after another into ravines and went rolling down the crags as a body of troops broke into their ranks and came to rescue the Emperor. The First Emperor was overjoyed. He looked and saw that it was Zhao Zilong of Changshan. At the time, Zhao Yun had been at Jiangzhou in the Riverlands. Hearing that Wu and Shu had gone to war, he had led his army out. Suddenly seeing flames towering into the sky across the southeast, Zhao Yun grew alarmed and sent scouts to investigate from afar. Learning unexpectedly that the First Emperor was trapped, he charged valiantly to the rescue. When Lu Xun heard that it was Zhao Yun, he immediately ordered his troops to withdraw. As Zhao Yun fought on, he suddenly encountered Zhu Ran and engaged him. Before a single bout was completed, Zhao Yun thrust Zhu Ran from his horse with one spear stroke, scattered the Wu troops, rescued the First Emperor, and fled toward Baidi City. The First Emperor said, “Though I have escaped, what is to become of my generals and soldiers?” Zhao Yun replied, “The enemy is behind us; we cannot delay. Your Majesty should enter Baidi City and rest for the moment. I shall lead the troops back to aid the other generals.” By then, the First Emperor had only a little over a hundred men remaining when he entered Baidi City. A later poet wrote these verses in praise of Lu Xun:

p.src: Meanwhile, Fu Tong, who had stayed behind to cover the retreat, was surrounded on all eight sides by the Wu army. Ding Feng shouted, “Countless soldiers of the Riverlands have died, and great numbers have surrendered. Your lord Liu Bei has already been captured. Now that your strength is exhausted and you stand alone, why do you not surrender at once?” Fu Tong rebuked him: “I am a general of Han! How could I ever surrender to the dogs of Wu?” Leveling his spear and spurring his horse, he led the Shu troops in a desperate fight to the death. For more than a hundred bouts he charged back and forth, but could not break free. Fu Tong sighed deeply and said, “My end has come!” As soon as he had spoken, blood poured from his mouth, and he died amid the Wu army. A later poet wrote these verses in praise of Fu Tong:

p.src: Cheng Ji, the libationer of Shu, rode alone to the riverbank and called upon the naval forces to meet the enemy. The Wu troops pursued close behind, and the naval forces scattered and fled. One of Cheng Ji’s officers cried, “The Wu troops are upon us! Libationer Cheng, flee quickly!” Cheng Ji said angrily, “Ever since I followed His Majesty to war, I have never once fled before the enemy!” Before he had finished speaking, the Wu troops swept down upon him. With no road of escape in any direction, Cheng Ji drew his sword and cut his own throat. A later poet wrote these verses in his praise:

p.src: At that time, Wu Ban and Zhang Nan had long been besieging the city of Yiling when Feng Xi suddenly arrived with word that the Shu army had been defeated. They therefore led their forces away to rescue the First Emperor, and only then was Sun Huan able to escape. While Zhang Nan and Feng Xi were marching, Wu troops charged at them from ahead, while Sun Huan sallied out of Yiling behind them, catching them between two attacks. Zhang Nan and Feng Xi fought desperately to break through, but could not escape and died amid the chaos of battle. A later poet wrote in their praise:

p.src: Wu Ban fought his way out through the encirclement, only to be pursued by Wu troops; fortunately, Zhao Yun met him and rescued him, escorting him back to Baidi. The Man king Shamoke was then fleeing alone on horseback when he encountered Zhou Tai. After fighting for more than twenty bouts, he was slain by Zhou Tai. The Shu generals Du Lu and Liu Ning both surrendered to Wu. Not the least of the grain, fodder, weapons, and equipment in the Shu camps remained. Countless Shu generals and soldiers of the Riverlands surrendered. Lady Sun was then in Wu. When she heard of the defeat at Xiaoting, a false report reached her that the First Emperor had died in battle. She drove her carriage to the riverbank, gazed westward and wept from afar, then threw herself into the river and died. Later generations built a shrine to her on the riverbank and called it the Shrine of the Valiant Lady. A later commentator wrote a poem lamenting her fate:

p.src: Now Lu Xun, having won a complete victory, led his triumphant troops westward in pursuit. When they were not far from Kui Pass, Lu Xun saw from horseback a murderous vapor rising skyward ahead, where the mountains met the river; he reined in his horse, looked back at his officers, and said, “There must be an ambush ahead. The army must not advance rashly.” He immediately withdrew more than ten li and drew up his formations on open ground to guard against the enemy; then he sent scouts ahead to investigate. They returned to report that no troops were stationed there. Lu Xun did not believe them; he dismounted, climbed a hill, and looked out, whereupon the murderous vapor rose again. Lu Xun ordered another careful search, but the scouts returned saying there was not a single man or horse ahead. As Lu Xun watched the sun sinking westward, the murderous vapor grew stronger. Still uncertain, he sent trusted men to investigate once more. They returned to report that there were only eighty or ninety heaps of scattered stones by the river, and neither men nor horses. Deeply perplexed, Lu Xun ordered some local people brought to learn what the place was called. Presently, several people arrived. Lu Xun asked, “Who piled up these scattered stones? And why does a murderous vapor rise from among them?” A local replied, “This place is called Yufupu. When Zhuge Liang entered the Riverlands, he brought troops here and arranged stones into a formation upon the strand; ever since, a cloudlike vapor has often risen from within.”

p.src: When Lu Xun had heard this, he mounted and led several dozen horsemen to inspect the stone formation; reining in on a hillside, he saw that entrances and gateways opened in every direction. Lu Xun laughed. “This is merely a trick to bewilder people. What use can it be?” He then led several riders down the slope and went straight into the stone formation to examine it. One of his officers said, “It is growing late. Pray return early, Commander.” Just as Lu Xun was about to leave the formation, a violent wind suddenly arose. In an instant, flying sand and hurtling stones blotted out heaven and earth. Fantastic rocks loomed jagged and gnarled like swords; banks of sand and walls of earth rose layer upon layer like mountains; the river roared and its waves surged with a sound like clashing swords and beating drums. Lu Xun cried in terror, “I have fallen into Zhuge Liang’s trap!” He hastened to turn back, but could find no way out. While he was bewildered and alarmed, an old man suddenly appeared before his horse and said with a smile, “Do you wish to leave this formation, General?” Lu Xun replied, “I beg you, venerable sir, to lead me out.” Leaning on his staff, the old man walked slowly on and passed straight out of the stone formation without hindrance, leading Lu Xun as far as the hillside. Lu Xun asked, “Who are you, venerable sir?” The old man answered, “I am Huang Chengyan, father-in-law to Zhuge Kongming. When my son-in-law entered the Riverlands, he laid out this stone formation and named it the Eightfold Formation. Its eight gates continually interchange according to the Dunjia principles: Rest, Life, Injury, Obstruction, Prospect, Death, Alarm, and Opening. It changes without limit at every hour of every day and is the equal of a hundred thousand elite soldiers. Before he left, he instructed me: ‘Later, a great general of Eastern Wu will become lost in this formation. Do not lead him out.’ Just now, from atop the crag, I saw you enter by the Gate of Death. I knew that you did not understand this formation and would surely be trapped by it. I have always delighted in doing good and could not bear to see you perish here, so I specially led you out through the Gate of Life.” Lu Xun asked, “Have you studied the method of this formation?” Huang Chengyan replied, “Its transformations are inexhaustible; it cannot be mastered.” Lu Xun hurriedly dismounted, bowed his thanks, and returned. Later, Du Fu of the Ministry of Works wrote a poem:

p.src: Back at his camp, Lu Xun sighed, “Kongming is truly the ‘Crouching Dragon’! I cannot equal him!” He then gave the order to withdraw. His attendants said, “Liu Bei’s army is defeated and his position hopeless; he is confined to defending a single city. This is the perfect moment to press our advantage and attack him. Why do you retreat now merely because you have seen the stone formation?” Lu Xun replied, “I am not retreating because I fear the stone formation. I judge that Cao Pi, ruler of Wei, is no less treacherous and cunning than his father. Now that he knows I am pursuing the Shu army, he will surely attack us while our defenses are empty. If I advance deep into the Western Riverlands, it will be difficult to withdraw in an emergency.” He therefore ordered one general to guard the rear while he led the main army back. Before they had been retreating for two days, urgent reports arrived from three quarters: “The Wei armies are advancing—Cao Ren from Ruxu, Cao Xiu from Dongkou, and Cao Zhen from Nanjun. Several hundred thousand troops in three columns are hastening day and night toward our borders. Their purpose is unknown.” Lu Xun laughed. “It is just as I expected. I have already sent troops to resist them.” Indeed:
